clue.text: Club that is metal-headed

indicators.note: headed says the metal word comes at the front, ahead of the abbreviation for that is

blocks.note: brass is an alloy metal
i.e., Latin id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A golf club described as having a metal head.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost literal: the old wooden club so named had a brass plate on its sole.
explanation.definitionFit: A brassie is an old name for a two-wood golf club, fitted with a brass sole plate.

clue.text: Boxing match - about nothing, however

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for however goes around the word for nothing

blocks.note: but and however are synonyms
O looks like zero, nothing; the run of letters at the end of the clue word about is a coincidence

explanation.surface: A boxing contest that came to nothing despite the hype.
explanation.definitionFit: A bout is a single contest or round of fighting, as in a boxing or wrestling match.

clue.text: Writer of a book strumpet found in honeypot

indicators.note: found in says the strumpet word sits inside the other word

blocks.note: taken as written
NT, the New Testament, is a book of the Bible
the sweet stuff tipped into a pot, as into a melting pot, so its letters are mixed
a trollop is an old word for a promiscuous woman

explanation.surface: An author whose book has a loose woman discovered in a honeytrap.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose clue: the pot is the only hint that the sweet stuff is stirred, and the strumpet goes in just before its last letter. The writer is the Victorian novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope was the Victorian novelist of the Barchester Chronicles, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Way fire ruined Galsworthy play

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked out of shape, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
the letters of fire rearranged

explanation.surface: A route ravaged by fire, as in a stage drama by Galsworthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife is a 1909 drama by John Galsworthy about an industrial strike at a tin-plate works.

clue.text: Musical prelude to dish served during dinner

blocks.note: first meaning: an opening piece of music or introduction to a ballet or opera
second meaning: a course in a meal, a main course in America and a middle course in older British use

explanation.surface: A little music played before the food comes to the table.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word means entrance, giving both an introductory musical piece and a course brought in at a meal.

clue.text: In which VIP may be put to sleep with top British journalist

definitions.text: In which VIP may be put to sleep

blocks.note: best and top both mean finest
B is the abbreviation for British
ed. is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A celebrity bedded down alongside a leading British reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put to sleep' suggests something sinister; it only means being bedded for the night as an honoured guest.
explanation.definitionFit: The finest bed in a household is reserved for honoured guests, so an important visitor sleeps there.

clue.text: Soft fabric transforming a bare hat

indicators.note: transforming means changing the form, so these letters are rearranged into new order

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: Some soft cloth turning a plain hat into something smarter.
explanation.definitionFit: Barathea is a fine woollen cloth with a broken rib weave, used for suits and uniforms.

clue.text: Sailor, for example, said to observe traveller

indicators.note: said tells us to go by the spoken word for observe rather than its spelling

blocks.note: to observe is to see, which is pronounced the same as the ocean
a farer is one who fares, or travels

explanation.surface: A sailor described as someone who watches travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: A seafarer is anyone who travels by ship, and a sailor is one example of such a person.

clue.text: Pot the noble stag to be a dinosaur

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used, with no separate signal word

explanation.surface: Shooting a fine stag looks like an old-fashioned pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal: the clue relies on the shuffle being spotted from the letter count and the odd phrasing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something old-fashioned and outmoded is called a dinosaur, a relic of earlier times.

clue.text: Academic bard out to follow island cricketer

indicators.note: out suggests the poet is put out of order, his letters disarranged
to follow says the pieces run in sequence, the island coming after

blocks.note: a don is a university lecturer
the letters of bard rearranged
the Isle of Man, between Britain and Ireland

explanation.surface: A university lecturer and a poet trailing after an island sporting hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Donald Bradman was the great Australian batsman, the highest-averaging Test cricketer of all time.

clue.text: Total put in circulation

blocks.note: first meaning: complete, absolute, as in a complete fool
second meaning: to pass coins or notes, especially counterfeit ones

explanation.surface: A sum of money issued for general use.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means complete or absolute; as a verb it means to issue currency, often forged.

clue.text: Sailor - one who wrote letters about train crash

indicators.note: a crash leaves the train's letters wrecked and jumbled
about means round, so the jumbled letters go around the letter writer

blocks.note: the letters of train rearranged
St Paul wrote the epistles, or letters, of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A seaman who once wrote letters concerning a rail disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' tempts one to think of a postman or author; it is the apostle who wrote the epistles.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarpaulin, the source of 'tar', was an old slang term for a seaman, from the tarred canvas they wore.

clue.text: It may reveal grounds for drinks on the coach

blocks.note: cups of coffee are drinks
a coach is a trainer; on places the drinks before it

explanation.surface: Something that offers a reason for refreshments served aboard a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' looks like reasons and 'coach' like a bus; they are the dregs of a brew and a sports coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A sieve for the brewed beverage catches and shows the leftover grounds after pouring.

clue.text: Fresh start when charlady works overtime?

definitions.note: read as three words, CLEANS LATE

blocks.note: first meaning: a record wiped of past faults
second meaning, split differently: a cleaner who does her job after hours

explanation.surface: A new beginning, as when the cleaner stays on after hours.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer after its sixth letter to get what a charlady does when she works overtime; a charlady is a cleaning woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiping a slate clean removes old marks, so the phrase means a record of past errors erased.

clue.text: Be idle when reciting short narrative poems

indicators.note: reciting means speaking out, so we want a word that sounds like the idling verb

blocks.note: to laze is to be idle

explanation.surface: Lounging about while reciting some brief verses.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay is a short lyric or narrative poem meant to be sung, as in Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome.

clue.text: Beaten by accident: fate indeed!

indicators.note: by accident means the letters of fate land in a random order

blocks.note: split as in deed: in signals that something goes inside, and deed is taken as written
the letters of fate rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation that losing by mischance was destiny after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'indeed' looks like one word; split it as in deed, with the jumbled fate going inside deed.
explanation.definitionFit: To be defeated is to be beaten in a contest, the past participle of the verb.

clue.text: Generally stupid, but frightfully sane about Ireland

indicators.note: frightfully suggests the letters of sane are put into a terrible state
about means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go round the island name

blocks.note: the letters of sane rearranged
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A remark that someone is usually foolish but terribly sane on the Irish question.
explanation.definitionFit: Anserine means goose-like, and geese stand for silliness, so the word also means foolish.

clue.text: Bears sin in a way for proud Balkan people?

indicators.note: in a way hints the letters are set out in another way or manner

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: A proud people of the Balkans bearing their sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Serbs, the people of Serbia in the Balkans, are known for strong national pride.

clue.text: One who sees to it that island, for example, backs king

indicators.note: backs says the abbreviation for for example is written backwards

blocks.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde, Scotland
e.g., exempli gratia
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone making sure an island supports its monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who arranges things is the person who organises them and sees to it that they happen.

clue.text: Fixed stake over volcano

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word for a fixed stake runs the other way

blocks.note: an ante is a fixed stake put in before a poker hand

explanation.surface: A set wager on a volcano erupting.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the active volcano on the east coast of Sicily, the highest in Europe.

clue.text: Capital entry revealing special gift

indicators.note: revealing says the answer is shown within the first words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: An outstanding entry showing a particular gift.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, a talent was also an ancient unit of money, so capital echoes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A talent is a natural aptitude or ability, a gift for doing something well.

clue.text: Withdraw and give up once more

blocks.note: first meaning: to move back or away
second meaning: to surrender again

explanation.surface: Retreating and surrendering a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: To recede is to move back; read with a hyphen it means to cede, or yield, again.

clue.text: Pirate couple allowed expensive bangle

blocks.note: Long John Silver is the pirate in Treasure Island
a brace is a pair
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A buccaneer pair permitted a costly piece of jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: A band of a precious metal worn round the wrist is a costly bangle; it is also old slang for handcuffs.

clue.text: Mind that may move in a certain direction

blocks.note: first meaning: look after, as in mind the children
second meaning: incline or lean towards something

explanation.surface: A mind that might wander off somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Mind looks like a noun; it is the verb meaning to look after.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to care for something and to have an inclination or go in a particular way.

clue.text: Utterly detest sailor - No. 1 mate, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters may be in some other order

blocks.note: AB, able seaman
taken as written
the numeral one looks like I
taken as written

explanation.surface: Loathing a seaman who might be first mate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No. 1 mate' reads as a ship's first officer; it is the letters of no, I and mate to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: To abominate is to loathe or abhor intensely, the strongest kind of hatred.

clue.text: Remove evidence of part of camera session

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a piece taken from inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Destroying the record of part of a photo shoot.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to rub out or delete something so that no trace of it remains.

clue.text: Numbers of teams

definitions.note: plural noun, cricket or football sides

blocks.note: first meaning: figures one more than ten
second meaning: football or cricket sides, each with that many players

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it asks for a head count; it is two meanings, since a side in football or cricket is named for its size.
explanation.definitionFit: The numeral after ten in the plural, and the usual name for sports sides fielding that many players.

clue.text: Conducted negotiations and supplied free drinks

blocks.note: first meaning: bargained, as one treats with an enemy
second meaning: paid for a round for others

explanation.surface: Someone held talks and stood everyone a round.
explanation.definitionFit: To treat with someone is to negotiate terms; to treat friends is to pay for their refreshments.
